title: Correlation and causation
meaning: Correlation measures how closely two numbers move together in a straight-line pattern. The correlation coefficient r runs from −1 to +1.
Analysts care because a strong correlation is easy to spot but is often mistaken for proof that one thing causes the other.
rule: r, the correlation coefficient, is between −1 and +1.
Sign: positive r means the two rise together; negative r means one falls as the other rises.
Strength: the closer r is to −1 or +1, the stronger the straight-line relationship. Near 0 means little or no linear relationship.
A correlation, however strong, does not show that one variable causes the other.

steps: The sign gives the direction: + means both rise together, − means one rises as the other falls.
The size, ignoring the sign, gives the strength: −0.8 is stronger than −0.4.
None of these values shows cause: a third factor, or chance, can link two measures.

trap.wrong: Concluding that one variable causes the other because r is large.
trap.why: Correlation is not causation. A confounding variable (a third factor) can drive both, as hot weather drives both ice cream sales and sunburn. A controlled experiment, such as an A/B test, is the usual way to show cause.

title: Linear regression: slope, intercept and R²
meaning: Linear regression draws the straight line that best fits a set of points, so you can predict one number from another.
Analysts care because the exam gives an equation such as sales = 50 + 4x and asks what the numbers mean or what it predicts.

formula.spoken: y equals m times x, plus b

symbols.meaning: the value used to predict it (the predictor)
the slope: how much y changes for each 1-unit rise in x; from two points, (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁)
the intercept: the value of y when x is 0
"R-squared", the share of the variation in y that the line explains, from 0 to 1; with one predictor it equals r × r

example.intro: A model predicts weekly orders y from sales calls x: y = 3x + 20, with r = 0.8.

table.caption: Predicted orders for three call counts
head: x (calls)
3x
y = 3x + 20

steps: The intercept b = 20: with no calls, the model predicts 20 orders.
The slope m = 3: each extra call adds 3 orders.
Slope from two points: (50 − 35) ÷ (10 − 5) = 15 ÷ 5 = 3, which matches m.
R² = r² = 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64: the line accounts for 64% of the variation in orders.

trap.wrong: Reading R² as the share of predictions that are right, or as proof that x causes y.
trap.why: R² is the share of the variation in y that the line explains. A high R² can still come from a confounder, and a prediction far outside the data range can be badly wrong.

title: Logistic regression
meaning: Logistic regression predicts the chance of a yes/no outcome, such as whether a customer will cancel, as a probability between 0 and 1.
Analysts care because the exam asks which model fits a question, and a yes/no outcome points to logistic, not linear, regression.
rule: The outcome has two values: yes or no, cancel or stay, fraud or genuine.
The model outputs a probability from 0 (surely no) to 1 (surely yes).
A threshold, usually 0.5, turns the probability into a class: at or above it is "yes".
Compare: linear regression predicts a number such as sales; logistic regression predicts the chance of a category.

example.intro: A churn model gives four customers a probability of cancelling. The team uses a threshold of 0.5.

steps: Compare each probability with the threshold: 0.5 or more is classed as "yes".
A and C are classed as "will cancel"; B and D as "will stay".
Raising the threshold to 0.7 would leave only A, catching fewer real cancellations but raising fewer false alarms.

trap.wrong: Choosing linear regression for a yes/no outcome.
trap.why: Linear regression predicts any number and can give impossible values like 1.3 or −0.2 for a yes/no question. Logistic regression keeps the output between 0 and 1.

title: Time series: trend, seasonality and moving averages
meaning: A time series is a measure recorded in time order, such as monthly sales. It can show a long-run trend, a repeating seasonal pattern, and random noise.
Analysts care because forecasting starts by separating these parts; a moving average smooths the noise so the trend shows.

formula.text: moving average = (sum of the last k values) ÷ k
formula.spoken: the moving average equals the sum of the last k values, divided by k

symbols.meaning: the window: how many recent periods to average, such as 3 months

symbols.symbol: sum of the last k values
symbols.meaning: add up the k most recent values
divide by the window size to get their mean

example.intro: Monthly sign-ups were 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80. Find the 3-month moving averages.
steps: Each moving average uses only the latest 3 months, so months 1 and 2 have none.
The average change is (80 − 40) ÷ 4 changes = 10 a month.
A simple trend forecast for month 6 is 80 + 10 = 90.

trap.wrong: Calling a pattern that repeats every year a trend.
trap.why: Seasonality repeats at the same time each period, such as every December. A trend is the long-run direction across many periods. A forecast that ignores seasonality will miss the December peak.
